title: The Divide Was Already There
author: Doan Winkel
source: How to Teach With AI (howtoteachwithai.substack.com), August 9, 2026
summary: Winkel poses the question 'Can AI strengthen -- not divide -- a campus?' and argues that AI does not create division in higher education so much as it audits and exposes fractures that already existed -- thin trust, performative assessment, adjunct labor precarity, and a public confidence in higher ed that had been declining since well before ChatGPT existed. He documents the scale of the integrity crisis (a 59% jump in AI misconduct cases at the University of Maryland, detection software that falsely flags non-native English speakers 61% of the time) alongside the labor and trust fallout at institutions like Sacramento State and the University of Colorado. Against this, he presents counter-evidence of campuses using AI well: Georgia State's Pounce chatbot cut summer melt by 21% largely among first-generation students, and a purpose-built Harvard physics tutor produced roughly double the learning gains of an equivalent active-learning class. His central argument is that AI's effect on any given campus depends entirely on the 'order of operations' -- whether a school buys tools and issues mandates first, as California State University did with disappointing results, or governs AI adoption together with faculty and students first, as Arizona State and Elon University did with stronger results. He closes with five concrete commitments for campus leaders: govern together, replace surveillance with redesigned assessment, protect unassisted thinking on purpose, reinvest saved time into human relationships, and put students at the table as co-authors of policy.
points: At the University of Maryland, AI-related misconduct cases jumped 59% in a single year, while a Stanford study found AI detectors falsely flag non-native English speakers as cheating 61% of the time.

Georgia State's Pounce chatbot cut 'summer melt' (admitted students who never enroll) by 21%, disproportionately helping first-generation and low-income students, while a purpose-built Harvard physics AI tutor produced roughly double the learning gains of the same lesson taught as in-class active learning.

California State University's $17 million-plus, procurement-first ChatGPT Edu rollout saw only 0.7% of students complete voluntary AI training and 52% of faculty report AI had negatively affected their teaching -- while Arizona State's faculty-governed rollout retained faculty senate support with no AI-linked faculty cuts.
Winkel's reframe: AI doesn't divide campuses, it audits them -- 'a technology this general doesn't inject values into an institution. It amplifies the values already there.'

His five-part test for campus leaders: govern deployments together, replace surveillance-based integrity policy with redesigned assessment, protect unassisted thinking on purpose, reinvest saved time into human relationships, and put students at the table as co-authors rather than subjects of policy.
quotes: AI didn't fracture the campus. It found the fractures. Whether it widens them or heals them is the most consequential choice higher education will make this decade.

At the University of Maryland, AI-related misconduct cases jumped 59% in a single year. In an Inside Higher Ed survey, 85% of students said they'd used generative AI for coursework in the past year -- one in five to write entire essays.
A University of Chicago study found something devastating this year: about 60% of students admit to using AI, but they estimate 90% of their peers do.

This is the reframe I want to offer: AI doesn't divide campuses. It audits them. It finds every place where trust was already thin, where work was already performative, where governance was already theater.
As of April 2026, 0.7% of students had completed the voluntary AI training. A systemwide survey of 94,000 people found 52% of faculty saying AI had negatively affected their teaching.
At Harvard, a physics course's purpose-built AI tutor -- engineered to scaffold, not solve -- produced roughly double the learning gains of the same lesson delivered as in-class active learning.

AI will not strengthen your campus, any more than a bell strengthens a congregation. People strengthen campuses -- when a moment of shared disruption gives them a reason to renegotiate, out loud, what they owe each other.
